# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Nissaggiya Pācittiya 5 (Bu-Vb Np5)

**ID:** Bu-Vb Np5

**Collection:** Vinaya

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** 5. Receiving a robe from a nun

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Nissaggiya Pācittiya 5, titled *Cīvarapaṭiggahana* ("Receiving a robe from a nun"), stipulates that a Buddhist monk who accepts robe-cloth from a nun must relinquish the cloth and confess the offense [SuttaCentral]. In the narrative framing accompanying the rule in the Pāli Vinaya, the Venerable Udāyin—a monk whose misbehavior frequently prompts the promulgation of monastic regulations—is described as having been left behind as a monastery caretaker (*āyasmā udāyi ohiyyako hoti vihārapālo*), an assignment that Jonathan Silk observes was likely no mark of honor in this monastic context [Silk 2008].

The rule corresponds to an established disciplinary norm across the Vinaya literature of early Buddhist schools. Curated parallels cataloged by SuttaCentral include the Pāli Bhikkhu Pātimokkha and Parivāra, Sarvāstivāda recensions in Chinese and Sanskrit, Mūlasarvāstivāda versions in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan, as well as Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṅghika, Lokottaravāda, Dharmaguptaka, Kāśyapīya, a Gāndhārī fragment, and parallel nuns' rules [SuttaCentral]. Automatically computed text-reuse data from DharmaNexus shows extensive internal phrasing shared with other Vinaya rules, particularly Nissaggiya Pācittiya 6, 4, 9, 25, 8, 17, and 27, Pācittiya rules 25 and 26, and Khandhaka passages such as the Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka (Kd 15) and Mahākhandhaka (Kd 1) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments of this text with Tibetan commentaries on the Prātimokṣa, specifically the *Pratimokṣasūtrapaddhati* (D4104) and the *Pratimokṣasūtraṭīkāvinayasamuccaya* (D4106) [DharmaNexus].

Modern translations listed on SuttaCentral include translations in five languages, among them a complete English version by Bhikkhu Brahmali [SuttaCentral].
